title: Biological computing
text:
Currently, biocomputers exist with various functional capabilities that include operations of Boolean logic and mathematical calculations.[1] Tom Knight of the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory first suggested a biochemical computing scheme in which protein concentrations are used as binary signals that ultimately serve to perform logical operations.[2] At or above a certain concentration of a particular biochemical product in a biocomputer chemical pathway indicates a signal that is either a 1 or a 0. A concentration below this level indicates the other, remaining signal. Using this method as computational analysis, biochemical computers can perform logical operations in which the appropriate binary output will occur only under specific logical constraints on the initial conditions. In other words, the appropriate binary output serves as a logically derived conclusion from a set of initial conditions that serve as premises from which the logical conclusion can be made. In addition to these types of logical operations, biocomputers have also been shown to demonstrate other functional capabilities, such as mathematical computations. One such example was provided by W.L. Ditto, who in 1999 created a biocomputer composed of leech neurons at Georgia Tech which was capable of performing simple addition.[2] These are just a few of the notable uses that biocomputers have already been engineered to perform, and the capabilities of biocomputers are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Because of the availability and potential economic efficiency associated with producing biomolecules and biocomputers—as noted above—the advancement of the technology of biocomputers is a popular, rapidly growing subject of research that is likely to see much progress in the future.

In March 2013, a team of bioengineers from Stanford University, led by Drew Endy, announced that they had created the biological equivalent of a transistor, which they dubbed a "transcriptor". The invention was the final of the three components necessary to build a fully functional computer: data storage, information transmission, and a basic system of logic.[3]

Parallel biological computing with networks, where bio-agent movement corresponds to arithmetical addition was demonstrated in 2016 on a SUBSET SUM instance with 8 candidate solutions.[4]

In July 2017, separate experiments with E. Coli published on Nature showed the potential of using living cells for computing tasks and storing information. A team formed with collaborators of the Biodesign Institute at Arizona State University and Harvard's Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering developed a biological computer inside E. Coli that responded to a dozen inputs. The team called the computer "ribocomputer", as it was composed of ribonucleic acid. Harvard researchers proved that it is possible to store information in bacteria after successfully archiving images and movies in the DNA of living E. coli cells.[5]

In 2021, a team led by biophysicist Sangram Bagh realized a study with E. coli to solve 2 x 2 maze problems to probe the principle for distributed computing among cells.[6,7]

In 2024, FinalSpark, a Swiss biocomputing startup, launched an online platform enabling global researchers to conduct experiments remotely on biological neurons in vitro.[8]

In March 2025, Cortical Labs revealed the CL1, world’s first commercial biological computer.[9]Made up of roughly 800,000 lab-grown human neurons grown on a silicon chip, code can be directly deployed to the neurons using the company's Biological Intelligence Operating System ("biOS").[10] The neurons can be kept alive for 6 months.[9] Cortical labs hopes the technology can be used in the medical field as well as compete with traditional AI systems.[9]

The Biological Computing Company (TBC) is a biological computing company headquartered in San Francisco.[11] TBC emerged from stealth in February 2026[12]. TBC uses living neurons to increase the efficiency of AI models, helping reduce inference cost and enhance coherent output[13]. The company uses a biological approach, developing software that applies computational principles observed in cultured neuronal networks to AI models.[14]
